_comment: Non-core extensions still allowed to run in-process instead of sandboxed.
This list may only SHRINK. It is enforced in CI by
scripts/declare_extension_runtime.py --check:
- a new extension may not be added (write it sandbox-clean instead);
- an entry that no longer needs the exemption must be deleted.
An entry leaves this list in one of two ways, and they are not equivalent:
1. Ported. The extension moves onto the capability bridge, its backend
stops importing ggg / core / basilisk / _cdk, "runtime":
"in_process" comes off its manifest, and the entry is deleted.
Privilege is actually removed.
2. Promoted to core. The extension is added to /core-extensions.json
because it administers the realm rather than runs on top of it, so
the survey stops considering it. Privilege is NOT removed — it is
reclassified as intentional, and moves from this audited list into
the trusted platform surface.
Only (1) is progress. (2) is a claim that sandboxing the extension was
never the right goal, and it should be argued per extension, not used to
make this number go down.
Each entry records the host roots that currently block sandboxing and the
issue tracking the port, so the ratchet count and the open-issue count
stay the same number.
Core/system extensions are not listed: they are never sandboxed by design.
Left this list via route (2) above rather than being ported. Recorded so
the drop in the count stays traceable to a decision.
task_monitor, access_manager and role_manager are the realm's execution,
governance and RBAC admin planes. Sandboxing them was never coherent: the
verbs it would take are the ones that confer authority, and a capability
to grant arbitrary permissions is not narrower than host access — it is
equivalent to it, wearing a verb name.
mundus_explorer is the weak one. It is a 161-line read-only federation
browser that was blocked only on the async outcall in #279, and #279 has
since landed (effect-style, see core/async_bridge.py). The reason it was
promoted no longer holds, so it is now the one entry here that is worth
reopening — it would be a small port on machinery that already exists.
